title: O Little Town of Bethlehem
description: Phillips Brooks's Christmas hymn to Lewis H. Redner's tune St. Louis, in Redner's four parts as Carols Old and Carols New (1916) prints them, for 2 to 4 singers: verses 1, 3 and 4, gentle and unhurried. Redner's chromatic chords colour "Beth-le-hem" and "Yet in thy dark streets shineth", and the bass holds a low B under "the everlasting Light".

credits.arrangement: Lewis H. Redner's four parts as Carols Old and Carols New (1916) prints them, adapted by Stackapella

licence.arrangement: Redner's four parts as Carols Old and Carols New (1916) prints them under his name alone (public domain: Redner died 1908; printed 1916; the book's editor Charles L. Hutchins died 1920), adapted for 2 to 4 beginners: his tune unchanged but for breaths; his chords kept; his bass kept but sung an octave lower from "by;" to "Light;" (G2 to B2 where he has G3 to B3, so it stays within a beginner bass's B-flat 3), and held on B under "The ev-er-last-", where he doubles the tune in all four voices (soprano and alto in unison, tenor and bass an octave below), which in two or three voices would be bare octaves; there the alto sings B3, D4 and E4 under the tune and the tenor G3 and B3 (our voicing); the alto and tenor revoiced in many other chords so the alto takes the chord's third under the tune and the tenor a note the alto leaves (for example the alto's C4 and B3 under "How still" and D-sharp 4 under "Light", as in the earliest known printing of 1874; F-sharp 4 under "see"; B3 under "si-", "by" and "met"; D4 under "Yet in thy" where he has G4); every part sung one note to a syllable (the tenor's quavers on "we", "lent" and "in", the bass's dotted figure on "si-lent" and the alto's quavers on "Are" each sung as one note); his last bass chord, printed as G2 and D3 together, sung as G2 with the tenor on D3, so the final chord is complete; and breaths written in for beginners; the bass sings "dream-less sleep" on A2, an octave lower, and the alto and tenor take Redner's own notes on "sleep" (A4, E4, C4) and on "dark streets" (F#4 and E4 in the alto, C4 and C#4 in the tenor). Accepted exceptions: the duet's bare fourth D5 over A4 on "dream-", Redner's 4-3 suspension resolving on "less"; its fourth E4 over B3 on "ev-" over the B pedal, where Redner prints bare octaves and no note under E4 carries the third; the weak-beat sevenths that pass without their third (beats 28 and 60.5 of each verse, the seventh resolving down); the tune's appoggiatura D5 over Redner's augmented C chord (53); the alto's falling A minor triad on "sleep"; and the soprano and alto more than an octave apart under the tune's leap to E5 on "met".
licence.source: Charles L. Hutchins, Carols Old and Carols New, for use at Christmas and other seasons of the Christian year (Boston: The Parish Choir, 1916), Carol 599, "O little town of Bethlehem!", p. 484, headed "Words by Bishop Phillips Brooks." and "L. H. Redner.", in four parts in G as printed and as written here, in crotchets (4/4) with a one-crotchet pickup; verses 1, 3 and 4 as printed under the music (the page prints four); read from Princeton Theological Seminary Library's copy at archive.org/details/carolsoldcarolsn00huth (scan page n515). Checked against The Hymnal, as authorized and approved for use by the General Convention of the Protestant Episcopal Church in the United States of America in the year of our Lord MCMXVI (New York: The Church Pension Fund, 1916), Hymn 78, "St. Louis", p. 99, headed "Lewis H. Redner, 1868." and signed "Phillips Brooks, 1868.", in G in minims (4/2), which prints the same tune and the same four parts wherever compared (archive.org/details/authoriz00epis, scan page n172; its index of composers gives Redner 1831-1908, scan page n69). The earliest known printing, The Church Porch: a service book and hymnal for Sunday schools, compiled and edited by William R. Huntington (New York: E. P. Dutton and Company, 1874; preface dated Worcester, Midsummer, 1874), No. 43, "St. Louis", "L. H. Redner.", in G in minims, verse 1 under the music and verses 2 to 4 below it (archive.org/details/churchporchservi00hunt, scan page n112), was compared: its tune differs in one note (B on "and" in "deep and dreamless", where the 1916 printings and we sing D) and its alto and tenor differ in places; we follow the 1916 form, the tune as it is sung today. Breaths written in for beginners: the lines that end on a crotchet ("hem!", "sleep", "neth", "years", and the same notes in verses 3 and 4) keep a quaver, and the next line's pickup comes in a semiquaver late; the held line ends ("lie;", "by;", "Light;", and "night." before the next verse) give up three quarters of a beat.
